summary:
Apurímac stands under the national framework of Peru. No Apurímac-specific trans statute, ordinance, incident series or enforcement finding appears in the sources attached to this record, and all three are national in scope; the operative rules for a visitor in the department are therefore the laws and enforcement patterns recorded at national level.

The most direct legal exposure concerns public restrooms. Bills 6506 and 8457, introduced by congressmen Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Muñante, were merged and approved unanimously by the congressional Women and Family Commission on 20 February 2025; the measure bars trans people from public restrooms that do not correspond to their sex at birth, with exceptions only for custody, situations requiring medical attention, or accompanying an elderly person, a child under 12 or a person with disabilities, and it bans 'ambiguous' bathroom signage. The congressional Plenary approved and exempted from a second vote on 2 April 2025 the bill whose article 5 bars any person from entering or using a public sanitary service that does not correspond to their 'biological sex', and it was enacted as Law 32331 on 13 May 2025. The package followed a July 2023 social-media complaint about gendered restroom labels at the Jorge Chávez airport.

The IDEHPUCP legal analysis by Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte of the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru concludes that article 5 violates the equal-treatment and non-discrimination principle of article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights, and that the stated aim of preventing child sexual abuse rests on a stigmatising stereotype that implicitly presents trans people as likely restroom harassers, while UN reporting shows trans people are more often victims than aggressors.

In practice, access to restrooms now turns on the personal judgment of security staff, potentially including identity-document checks, a consequence flagged by LGTBIQ activist Gianna Camacho; she also notes there is no record of sexual assault by trans women in women's restrooms. The restriction reaches private premises as well as public facilities: a consumer-protection body dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against a gym that enforced the policy, and on television presenter Ana María Salcedo of Willax TV publicly harassed Susel Paredes, the first openly lesbian member of Congress, telling her to 'go use the men's room'.

Hate-crime protection is absent. Peru's Congress voted in 2017 to strip LGBT protections from the new Penal Code's hate-crime provisions, with Popular Force and Alliance for Progress members carrying the repeal after an April Constitutional Committee vote and amid a petition claiming one million signatures. The outcome leaves Peru one of only three countries in South America, with Paraguay and Guyana, lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in hate-crime law.

Violence against trans people is documented and under-recorded. The Observatorio de Derechos TLGBI annual report records 54 murders of TLGBI people and 170 rights-violation cases over 2020-2023, with trans women more than half the homicide victims (30), followed by 23 gay men and one lesbian; killings rose to 19 in 2023, of whom 12 were trans women, from 13 in 2022, 10 in 2021 and 12 in 2020, many committed with cruelty. Among the cases is the February 2023 gang abduction of trans sex worker Rubí Torres Silvano, 31, in central Lima and her killing in Carabayllo with about 30 gunshots as part of an extortion scheme. A 2024 report found hate crimes rising with trans women most affected, and co-author Gianna Camacho, a trans journalist and human-rights defender, stressed that recorded figures are only a sub-registry.

Accountability has come once, after long litigation. In December 2025 three police officers, Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León, were sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment for the rape and torture of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, nearly 20 years after the attack. It was Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and, per BBC News Mundo, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history, reaching the Court through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.
tangentialFactors:
The Inter-American Court of Human Rights held in Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and that states must guarantee trans people's full rights. IDEHPUCP records that the bathroom provision breaches that standard, and also documents dehumanising comparisons made on the floor of Congress by congressman Lizarzaburu.

The exclusion of LGBT people from hate-crime coverage places Peru alongside only Paraguay and Guyana in South America, a regional outlier position that shapes what protection a trans visitor can expect from prosecutors and courts.

A July 2025 Lima constitutional court, acting on an activist legal challenge, ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional, showing that judicial review remains available even as the legislature restricts access.

Speech and association are constrained by the same legislative package. Vague child-protection articles in the April 2025 law, including an article 4 ban on media and advertising content, enable censorship of identity, artistic and educational material, and the minimum sentence for obscenity was raised from three to four years; Human Rights Watch states that child protection is a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people.
localsOnly:
Residents carry the burden of the 2017 Penal Code repeal in their daily dealings with state institutions: the removal was engineered inside Congress after an April Constitutional Committee vote, and no national hate-crime provision now covers anti-LGBT or anti-trans motivation.

Two protective developments are on record for people living in Peru. In June 2024 health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described as a step toward dignity for trans patients in healthcare settings, and the July 2025 constitutional court ruling against an anti-equality decree reopened a legal route that residents can use.

The violence statistics are themselves incomplete. The 170 rights-violation cases logged between 2020 and 2023 include state violence and incitement to discrimination, with 61 denuncias recorded in 2020 alone, and Gianna Camacho states that the published figures are only a sub-registry of actual incidents.

Institutions involved in contesting the rules include IDEHPUCP, whose analysis was written by Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte, and the Observatorio de Derechos TLGBI, whose 2024 report supplied the homicide series. The bathroom bills were advanced by the congressional Women and Family Commission and originate with Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Muñante, both of Honor y Democracia.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Apurímac-specific finding exists in this record: the three attached sources are national in scope, and no departmental ordinance, regional government directive, police report or incident series for Apurímac was located. The national law is treated as governing the department because no sub-national instrument displaces it, not because a local application has been documented.

Whether Apurímac's regional or municipal authorities have issued their own implementing rules for public facilities, or whether any complaint under Law 32331 has been filed in the department, remains unresolved and not sourced.

The homicide and rights-violation counts are national totals for 2020-2023; a breakdown by department, including Apurímac, is not sourced, and the named killing in this record occurred in Lima.

The consumer-protection dismissal of the gym complaint and the television harassment of Susel Paredes are reported as national-level events; no evidence of comparable private-venue enforcement in Apurímac was located, and the practical intensity of restroom screening in the department is unknown.
